name: The Nintendo PlayStation
title: The 360,000 Dollar Ghost Console
claims: The Super NES CD-ROM, or SNES CD, was a proposed video game platform developed by Nintendo via joint ventures with Sony and Philips | [1]
The Sony project was a dedicated all-in-one unit under the name "PlayStation" using the Super Disc format | [1]
The Philips project was an add-on unit for the SNES that used the Nintendo Disc (ND) format | [1]
All of these projects were cancelled shortly after Nintendo backed out of both collaborations a few years into development | [1]
Sony developed its own console using the PlayStation name afterwards | [1]
Philips gained licenses for some Nintendo properties for its CD-i platform, many of which were unsuccessful and poorly received | [1]
Nintendo would not release an optical disc-based console of their own until 2001 with the GameCube | [1]
Released in 1990, the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) was Nintendo's entry into the fourth generation of video game consoles | [1]
The SNES outsold its competitors, the TurboGrafx-16/PC Engine and the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive, becoming the most popular console of that generation | [1]
NEC was the first to use CD technology with its TurboGrafx-CD/PC Engine CD-ROM² add-on in 1988 | [1]
Sega followed with their Sega CD/Mega-CD add-on in 1991 | [1]
Sony engineer Ken Kutaragi became interested in video game development after observing his daughter play games on Nintendo's Famicom | [1]
Without full corporate approval, Kutaragi secretly designed the S-SMP audio chip for Nintendo's Super NES | [1]
Kutaragi was nearly fired for doing so, but received support from Sony executive Norio Ohga | [1]
Kutaragi proposed a CD-ROM drive for the Super NES, claiming the drive would be used for multimedia purposes rather than games | [1]
Development of the Sony-branded PlayStation began in late 1988 | [1]
The PlayStation was designed to support both Super NES cartridges and the Super Disc CD format | [1]
Contemporaneous plans reportedly called for the integration of the Super FX coprocessor developed by Argonaut Games | [1]
Jez San recalled that the chip was discussed as part of early technical proposals during negotiations | [1]
Sony would retain control over the Super Disc format, software licensing, and exclusive music and movie content | [1]
Nintendo president Hiroshi Yamauchi found the terms unacceptable | [1]
Yamauchi was wary of Sony demanding game developers use its expensive proprietary audio tools for the S-SMP | [1]
Yamauchi suspected Nintendo was being used to advance Sony's ambitions of launching its own console | [1]
Yamauchi dispatched Minoru Arakawa and Howard Lincoln to the Netherlands to negotiate with Philips | [1]
The Philips deal was meant to give Nintendo back its software stranglehold and gracefully f--k Sony | [1]
Nintendo's intent to go with Philips was publicly announced two days before CES in a May 1991 Seattle Times report | [1]
At CES in June 1991, Sony publicly unveiled its hybrid SNES-compatible PlayStation | [1]
The next day, Nintendo revealed its partnership with Philips, referred to by journalists as "the greatest ever betrayal" | [1]
During the period after CES 1991, two to three hundred PlayStation prototypes were produced, and software development was underway | [1]
In early 1992, the companies reached a deal allowing Sony to produce SNES-compatible hardware while Nintendo controlled game profits | [1]
Kutaragi persuaded Sony to abandon the Super NES CD-ROM and pursue a standalone next-generation console | [1]
Sony cut all ties to Nintendo in May 1992 | [1]
The Nintendo-Philips partnership led to an add-on featuring a 32-bit coprocessor and a new CD format based on CD-ROM XA known as the Nintendo Disc (ND) | [1]
Nintendo reportedly canceled the project quietly as late as September 1993 | [1]
The Sony PlayStation prototype model number was SFX-100 | [1]
Photos of these prototypes resurfaced in the 2000s and were featured in an Edge article in April 2009 | [1]
In July 2015, one prototype was reportedly found, abandoned by Ólafur Jóhann Ólafsson during his time at Advanta | [1]
Terry Diebold acquired the device as part of a lot during Advanta's 2009 bankruptcy auction | [1]
Benjamin Heckendorn's 2016 tear-down video showed the prototype featured two Super NES controller ports, a cartridge slot, and a tray-loading dual-speed CD-ROM drive | [1]
The prototype featured RCA composite jacks, S-Video, RFU DC OUT, a multi-out AV output port, front headphone jack, a serial port labelled "NEXT", and one expansion port | [1]
The system was confirmed operational, missing its original power supply, requiring a third-party power supply | [1]
The unit plays Super Famicom cartridges and its included test cartridge, but audio output and CD drive were non-functional | [1]
It came with a Sony/PlayStation-branded version of the standard Super Famicom controller (model number SHVC-005) | [1]
Homebrew software like Super Boss Gaiden was developed for the console | [1]
In March 2016, RetroCollect reported receiving a functional disc boot ROM for the SNES-based PlayStation from an anonymous source | [1]
Diebold gave the unit to Benjamin Heckendorn in 2016, who posted a tear-down video and technical specifications | [1]
Heckendorn identified and replaced faulty on-board components in 2017, fixing audio and CD drive issues | [1]
Heckendorn created a custom power supply based on the original PlayStation and modified the unit to use a Sony Walkman power connector | [1]
Heckendorn showed Super Famicom and SNES games, audio CDs, and homebrew working on the system | [1]
The prototype was auctioned off by Diebold to Greg McLemore in February 2020 for $360,000 | [1]
The sale earned a Guinness World Record for the "most expensive videogame console sold online" | [1]
In March 2025, Kutaragi showcased one of the prototype units that he has kept inside his closet for storage, in much better condition | [1]
The Super NES CD-ROM System add-on used a caddy loading drive accepting discs in enclosed caddy cases | [1]
The add-on CD drive operated at single (1x) and double (2x) speeds | [1]
Nintendo decided to use a new 32-bit RISC processor (SCCP), reported to be an NEC V810 at 21.47727 MHz, with additional RAM, ROM, and a coprocessor called "HANDS" | [1]
Super Boss Gaiden was released by German duo Chrono Moogle and Dieter Lazer in Summer 2016 | [2]
The game plot follows Sony's President on a rampage across Sony Headquarters after the last SNES CD prototype falls to the general public | [2]
The game has a regular SFC ROM for standard SNES and an image file to run on the SNES CD prototype | [2]

sources.title: Someone Has Actually Made A Game Which Works On The SNES PlayStation | Nintendo Life
